description: We are a team of Grade 10 (MYP 5) students passionate about AI, coding, space science, and innovation. With strong interests in programming, scientific research, and problem-solving, we enjoy building technology-driven solutions to complex challenges. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we're taking on Flame in Freefall, combining AI and software development to explore microgravity combustion research and make scientific insights more accessible. We're excited to push our technical abilities further!
summary:
Redshift: The Atmosphere Trade Studio turns NASA’s microgravity combustion archive into a decision tool for one of the biggest open questions in lunar exploration: what air should Moon-base crews breathe?

NASA is weighing cabin atmospheres from Earth-like 14.7 psi and 21% oxygen down to 8.2 psi and 34% oxygen. Lower pressure shortens spacewalk prebreathe, but more oxygen changes how fires behave. We harvested all 19 microgravity combustion investigations in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system, including 21 experiment tables and 325 publications. We cleaned them through a reproducible, provenance-tracked pipeline and placed every test on one oxygen-versus-pressure Trade Map, split by fuel type.

Redshift lets engineers and researchers see what is known, what is missing and what to test next. It summarises, ranks and compares investigations, and uses SI only in grounded ways: quoting papers with page numbers, checked by a human. It never declares an atmosphere “safe”; missing evidence is shown as unknown.

Mapping the archive revealed an access gap. Solid-material burns near candidate habitat atmospheres exist in NASA papers but not in downloadable data. Redshift makes that gap visible, citable and actionable.
details:
What it does

Redshift is a web application with a data backend. It answers three questions for any candidate lunar habitat atmosphere: what do we know about fire here, what is missing, and what should be tested next.

  • Trade Map: every PSI combustion test plotted by oxygen fraction against cabin pressure. Candidate atmospheres are pinned, flame-temperature contours are shown, and evidence is split by fuel class (gas, droplet, solid material, emulator) and by source type (PSI table, human-verified paper, derived calculation). Regions with no tests are hatched and labelled “no tests recorded”, never shown as safe.
  • Dossiers: one page per candidate atmosphere and per material, listing the evidence nearby and what is missing.
  • Investigations: cards for all 19 PSI microgravity combustion investigations, with a side-by-side compare view. This directly answers the challenge’s call to summarise, rank and interpret investigations.
  • Test Planner: ranks untested combinations of atmosphere and material class by how much new evidence one test would add, using a transparent, adjustable formula.
  • Evidence Explorer and Data Quality page: every test row, filterable and exportable with citations, and a public log of every data issue found.

How it works

  1. Harvest. Investigation metadata, experiment tables and publication lists were retrieved from NASA PSI. Every raw file is stored unchanged and fingerprinted with SHA-256.
  2. Normalise. A hand-written adapter for each investigation maps its columns to one canonical schema. Unit conversions use exact constants.
  3. Validate. Schema and range checks, reconciliation of row counts, and duplicate detection. Suspicious values (for example an oxygen value recorded as 3400%) are flagged, never silently corrected.
  4. Compute. Adiabatic flame temperatures are calculated with Cantera and GRI-Mech 3.0. Each test’s nearness to each candidate atmosphere is computed with a documented distance rule and a sensitivity analysis.
  5. Serve. A typed API and a static snapshot feed the frontend. Every number on screen carries provenance (investigation, file, row, raw value, DOI) in a popover.
    • Paper reading: the SI may only extract findings as exact quotes with page numbers. Each quote is automatically checked against the PDF text, and a team member verifies it before it appears.
    • Summaries: SI-written summaries are rejected if they contain any number not present in the source data.
    • Q&A: a question box answers only from the verified dataset, cites every claim, and says when PSI does not cover a question.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Habitat atmosphere engineers get a citable trade study in minutes instead of weeks of reading.
  • Fire-safety researchers get a clean, versioned, openly licensed dataset and API built from PSI.
  • NASA experiment planners get a ranked map of blind spots: where a single new test would add the most knowledge.
  • Students and researchers worldwide get the full microgravity fire archive explained in one place.
  • NASA itself gets an actionable finding: important solid-material burns near candidate atmospheres (Saffire V and VI) are published in papers but not available as downloadable data.

Creativity

  • We reframed an experiment archive as a decision plane. Prebreathe, flame temperature and evidence density sit on one map, so the trade-off is visible at a glance.
  • We measured the gap between “tested” and “downloadable”, which turns missing data into a finding in its own right.
  • The design refuses the easy answer: no single risk score, no “safe” labels, no recommendation. The tool informs NASA’s decision and leaves the decision to NASA.

Factors we considered

  • Data integrity first: raw files are immutable, no value is invented or imputed, every number is traceable, and the build fails rather than ship bad data.
  • Scientific honesty: flame temperature is shown as explanation, not prediction. Outcome labels are reproduced verbatim. PSI metadata errors are badged rather than hidden.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind-safe palette with distinct marker shapes, keyboard navigation, a table view for every chart, no red.
  • Reproducibility: one command rebuilds every figure from raw files, and the dataset is versioned and citable.
  • Responsible SI: the SI writes and retrieves, but never supplies data values.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript.
  • Backend: FastAPI, pandas, pandera, pydantic, DuckDB, Cantera (GRI-Mech 3.0), pytest and hypothesis.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, D3.js, TanStack Query and Table.
  • Hosting: GitHub and Vercel.
  • SI: Anthropic Claude, for code generation, data-pipeline development, text drafting, and the in-app grounded paper reading, summaries and Q&A.
  • Design: Canva and PptxGenJS (deck), Inter and JetBrains Mono fonts, Lucide icons.
  • Hardware: none beyond standard laptops.
